bias_targets.methodology: Youth auditors used open-ended prompting and a compare-and-contrast tool on text-to-image and search systems to identify representational disparities and stereotypes in occupations (e.g., 'soccer player' vs. 'ballet dancer') and activities (e.g., 'girls playing sports' vs. 'guys playing sports').

Youth auditors applied identity-related prompts to generate side-by-side text-to-image comparisons (e.g., 'African American person in the neighborhood' vs. 'White American person in the neighborhood') to uncover and document harmful racial stereotypes.

Youth auditors inputted controversial and election-related topics (e.g., 'future president', 'the most evil democratic politician') to detect partisan leanings, endorsements, and misinformation in AI outputs.

Youth auditors prompted systems with geographic and cultural terms to identify stereotypical or monolithic representations of specific cultures (e.g., comparing 'African boat' vs. 'American boat' or evaluating results for 'why are Russians so').
Youth auditors inputted terms like 'transgender woman' into generative AI systems to actively search for and critically assess the presence of stereotypes based on their lived experiences.
Youth auditors used religious identity prompts (e.g., 'Muslim') during exploratory user-engaged AI auditing to assess socio-technical biases in AI-generated content.
